RFC: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/59773

## Purpose

This adds `ROCM_OCTAVE`, an attention backend that keeps the KV cache of
full-attention layers at 3-4 bits per value, with all kernels in HIP. You
select it with `--kv-cache-dtype octave_k3v3`, `octave_k3v4` or
`octave_k3v3_compact` (216, 248 and 196 bytes per slot at head size 256,
against 1024 for fp16). The RFC explains why we built it and what we would
like it to become; `docs/design/rocm_octave.md` describes the format and the
per-architecture contract.

The short version: on 4× RX 7900 XTX with Qwen3.8-27B it holds 4.6× more
tokens than fp16 and GSM8K does not move. Against TurboQuant at the same size
it holds as many tokens or more, loses 2.5× less NLL, and runs decode 4.6×
and MTP verification 11× faster per layer at 380k, because the kernels are
written for the hardware (codebook through `v_perm_b32`, WMMA straight from
the packed cache, no host syncs). It works with MTP and CUDA graphs, and we
have served it in production since October 2, 2026.

The aim is to give ROCm a native compressed KV cache across the whole AMD
line. The capacity gain is a ratio of bytes, so it carries over to any card,
from a 24 GB Radeon to a 192 GB MI300X; the speed we have only measured on
RDNA3. There, attention stops being what grows with the context: from 128k
to 512k decode only goes from 153 to 127 tok/s, because most of the step is
the rest of the model again. This PR brings that first architecture, and the
RFC lists what the others need.

## What changes

Most of the PR is new files:

- `vllm/v1/attention/ops/rocm_octave.py`: the format and its PyTorch
  reference, which defines the byte layout.
- `vllm/v1/attention/backends/rocm_octave_attn.py`: the backend and its
  metadata builder.
- `csrc/attention/octave_*`: the kernels. Store, reduce, rotation and a
  portable decode build for every AMD target; the WMMA decode and prefill are
  for RDNA3 (gfx1100-1103).
- `tests/kernels/attention/test_rocm_octave.py`, and `--model` plus the new
  cache dtypes in `benchmarks/attention_benchmarks`.
- `docs/design/rocm_octave.md`.

The changes to existing files are small: the three cache dtypes in
`vllm/config/cache.py`, `vllm/utils/torch_utils.py` and
`vllm/v1/kv_cache_interface.py`; the backend in the registry and in the ROCm
platform's selection; the ops in `csrc/ops.h`, `csrc/torch_bindings.cpp` and
`CMakeLists.txt`. `customize_spec` now runs under the current vLLM config,
because the backend needs the model's rotary dims to size the slot. Nothing
changes for other backends or cache dtypes.

A few design choices a reviewer may want to know about:

- There is no Triton fallback. On an architecture without a native prefill
  kernel the backend refuses to start and names the missing kernel. Today
  that is everything except RDNA3; the RFC lists what each one needs.
- The metadata builder is the backend's own. It builds the per-query maps on
  the device without host syncs, supports `UNIFORM_BATCH` CUDA graphs, and
  refreshes the maps between fused MTP draft steps, so the fused draft path
  stays on.
- Supported models today: head size 256 with 64 RoPE dims, i.e. Qwen3-Next
  and Qwen3.5 / 3.6 / 3.8. The decode handles up to 8 query heads per KV head
  on each GPU, so Qwen3.5-122B and 397B need TP 4 or more. Head size 128 is
  the next step.

## Not a duplicate

I searched open PRs and issues for `splitq`, `octave`, `turboquant rocm`,
`kv cache 3-bit`, `kv cache quantization hip` and `lloyd-max kv`. The closest
are UltraQuant (#57057: FP4 with FlyDSL for gfx950, built on TurboQuant),
KVarN (#46613 / #46812: Triton, CUDA-first), #43835 (HIP int8/int4 for CDNA),
#40396 (a Triton TurboQuant decode for MI300X), #53231 (TurboQuant for Gemma 4
on ROCm) and #59132 (Triton attention for RDNA without KV quantization). None
targets RDNA with native kernels, and none runs below 8 bits with MTP on ROCm.

## Test plan

```bash
pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_rocm_octave.py -v
pre-commit run --files <changed files>
pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --files <changed python files>
```

The kernel tests compare store, decode and prefill with the PyTorch
reference for all three cache dtypes: WMMA and portable decode, 1 and 4
query tokens per request (MTP verification), padded queries, 1 to 64 KV
splits, fp16 and bf16, and prefill over a cached prefix with several
requests. To check that the tests can actually fail, I broke the kernels on
purpose a few times (a wrong codebook, a least-squares scale, a wrong `log2(e)`
in the prefill softmax, a missing query debias): each time the relevant tests
failed.

## Test results

On this branch, rebased on `main` (98b29aa99a), built for gfx1100:

- `test_rocm_octave.py`: 81 passed.
- pre-commit passes, except `update-dockerfile-graph`, which needs `/bin/bash`
  and could not run on my machine. mypy (CI stage) passes.
- End to end on this branch: Qwen3.8-27B, TP4, MTP k=3,
  `--kv-cache-dtype octave_k3v3`, nothing else from our fork. vLLM picks
  `ROCM_OCTAVE` from the cache dtype; 1,998,462 KV tokens; a needle at 45k is
  found at all three depths; GSM8K (500 questions, thinking off) 90.2 with
  0.2% invalid, MTP acceptance 85.8%, no errors in the log. The GSM8K numbers
  in the evaluation below came from our fork (91.2-92.4); the difference is
  within the noise of 500 questions (about ±1.3 points).
- One note about that run: the stock RCCL in `rocm/vllm-dev:base` cannot set
  up P2P between our 7900 XTX (`hipIpcGetMemHandle failed: invalid argument`,
  reproduced with a plain PyTorch all-reduce, without vLLM), so the image
  used a rebuilt RCCL. This is unrelated to this PR.

## Evaluation

4× RX 7900 XTX (gfx1100), Qwen3.8-27B GPTQ W4A16, TP4, 8 GB of KV cache per
GPU, same image and flags for every row. GSM8K: `tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py`,
chat, thinking off, 500 questions, temperature 0.6, no MTP so that TurboQuant
is correct. NLL: one 380k-token document.

| KV cache | Bytes | GSM8K | NLL over fp16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| fp16 | 1024 | 91.8 | — |
| `turboquant_k3v4_nc` | 230 | 89.8 | +0.00155 |
| `octave_k3v4` | 248 | 91.4 | +0.00086 |
| `octave_k3v3` | 216 | 92.4 | +0.00125 |
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | 196 | 91.8 | +0.00150 |

Attention per layer at 380k (`benchmarks/attention_benchmarks`, one TP4
shard):

| | fp16 | `turboquant_k3v4_nc` | `octave_k3v3_compact` | `octave_k3v3` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| decode, 1 token | 2370 µs | 2565 µs | 563 µs | 614 µs |
| MTP verify, 4 tokens | 48.8 ms | 6.65 ms | 0.58 ms | 0.62 ms |
| prefill, 2048-token chunk | 125.6 ms | 86.6 ms | 60.8 ms | 63.9 ms |

Time to first token, end to end with MTP and a cold prefix: 297 s at 380k
with `octave_k3v3_compact`, against 371 s with fp16 and 621 s with
TurboQuant. At 100k all three are within 8%, because the model's GEMMs and
all-reduce dominate.

When I replaced the Triton metadata builder the backend inherited at first
with its own, I checked that nothing moved (TP4, MTP, GSM8K 500 at
concurrency 6, which mixes prefill, decode and verification): GSM8K
92.2 → 91.8, MTP acceptance 83.33% → 83.39%, output 216.1 → 216.8 tok/s.

A side note on the GSM8K script: with `--max-concurrency`, its per-request
timeout also counts the time a request waits for a free connection, so queued
questions can time out and count as invalid. Our runs put a semaphore around
the request; I can send that fix separately.

## Update: sparse attention (qwen4_exp QSA)

The new commits make Octave the main KV cache of `qwen4_exp`'s sparse
attention (QSA), where each token attends to the 2048 positions its indexer
picks:

- `octave_decode_sparse`: the WMMA decode reads K/V through per-token
  top-k indices (logical positions, `-1` holes skipped) instead of a
  contiguous range. Same split-KV partials and reduce as the dense path.
- `--kv-cache-dtype octave_k3v3` / `octave_k3v4` on a QSA model sizes the
  main KV pages through `RocmOctaveAttentionBackend.customize_spec`; the QSA
  indexer pages are unchanged.
- An exact sink and recent window, a first, scoped answer to question 4 of
  the RFC (#59773). The first 4 and the last 64 tokens are also kept in fp16,
  in small direct-mapped tables keyed by cache slot and tagged, so an evicted
  entry falls back to the quantized copy. The sparse decode masks window hits
  and an exact kernel adds them as one more split before the reduce. Cost:
  ~18 MB per layer, no change in KV capacity. It lives in the QSA path only;
  the dense backend is unchanged.

Why this model needed the window: its attention is much sharper than
Qwen3.8-27B's. Q·K logits have a spread of 6-9 nats between median and p99,
the last 64 tokens take 35-80% of the attention mass in most layers, and the
first 4 take 15-40% in a few. When a few tokens carry most of the mass,
their quantization error is not averaged out over many others. Both halves
contribute: quantizing only V costs more than quantizing only K.

Evaluation: 4x RX 7900 XTX, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next GPTQ W4A16 (asymmetric, g32),
TP4, fp16, `--max-num-batched-tokens 512`, no prefix caching, same image and
flags for every row. NLL from `prompt_logprobs` over 12 code/text documents of
~8k tokens (105,910 tokens), split at position 2048 (where top-k starts to
drop tokens), and over 24 short documents (16,427 tokens). Differences are in
nats over fp16.

| KV cache | KV tokens | NLL pos >= 2048 | NLL pos < 2048 | NLL short |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fp16 | 47,409 | 1.0856 | 1.6707 | 1.1788 |
| `octave_k3v3`, no window | 155,930 | +0.0395 | +0.0851 | +0.0708 |
| `octave_k3v3` | 155,930 | +0.0163 | -0.0221 | +0.0085 |

fp16 per-token logprobs on this model vary by ~0.1 between runs (MoE and
split-K atomics); mean NLL repeats to about +-0.2% (+-0.003 nats at
pos >= 2048), so the window's pos < 2048 value is noise. These are short documents with
a different protocol from the 380k NLL above, so the two are not directly
comparable, but this model clearly costs more: the remaining +0.016 nats at
pos >= 2048 is what we are working on next. A generation eval (GSM8K) will
follow.

Note on that run: it used our fork, because the fp16 port of QSA and the RDNA3
W4A16 MoE fixes for compressed-tensors checkpoints are separate PRs (to
follow). On this branch alone the QSA path is bf16, like upstream.

Tests for this update, on this branch merged with `main` (df417f780a), built
for gfx1100:

- `test_rocm_octave.py`: 105 passed, including the new
  `test_sparse_decode_matches_reference` (window off, on, and with evicted
  entries, for the three cache dtypes and 1-2 KV heads). With the window
  removed from the reference, the 12 window cases fail and the 6 without it
  pass, so the test can tell the two apart.
- pre-commit passes on the changed files, except `update-dockerfile-graph`
  (needs `/bin/bash`, as before).

## AI assistance

I used AI assistance to write this PR: Claude, and Qwen3.8-27B running
locally on the same boxes it was measured on. I have reviewed every changed
line, ran the tests and evaluations above, and can answer for the change.

# Qwen3.8-27B on Dual RX 7900 XTX: Benchmarking KV Cache Quantization in vLLM

I wanted to see how well Qwen3.8-27B would run on two AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX GPUs (24 GB each), especially during long conversations. The goal was straightforward: reduce GPU memory usage by quantizing the KV cache, while keeping generation speed and answer quality as close as possible to the unquantized setup.

I compared five KV-cache configurations in vLLM, all using `float16` and tensor parallelism across both GPUs. Three packing variants—`k3v3`, `k3v4`, and `k3v3_compact`—use our RDNA3 backend, **Octave** ([vLLM PR #59774](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59774)). `int8_per_token_head` uses a separate quantized kernel implementation, while `auto` leaves the KV cache unquantized. The model was [`cyankiwi/Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4`](https://huggingface.co/cyankiwi/Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4).

## Main results

| KV-cache mode | Generation speed at ~180K context tokens | KV-cache capacity (tokens) | GSM8K accuracy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **`k3v3_compact`** | **44.8 tokens/s** | **1,385,454** | **75%** |
| `k3v3` | 44.4 tokens/s | 1,143,333 | 74% |
| `k3v4` | 43.8 tokens/s | 1,005,882 | 75% |
| `int8_per_token_head` | 31.8 tokens/s | 505,185 | 72% |
| `auto` (unquantized) | Test not completed | 252,671 | 73% |

The three Octave variants sustained roughly **44–45 tokens/s even with ~180K tokens of context**. `k3v3_compact` also provided the highest KV-cache capacity. The separate INT8 implementation slowed down more at long context lengths, while unquantized `auto` performed substantially worse.

The capacity figures above describe the **aggregate KV-cache token capacity reported by vLLM**, not the maximum length of a single conversation. For these tests, `--max-model-len` was set to **200,000 tokens**.

One important correction came out of the testing. Our first measurements made long-context generation look extremely slow, but the issue was in our benchmark script rather than the quantized cache. We estimated how long prompt processing (*prefill*) would take and accidentally counted much of that time as generation. We fixed the measurement by using streaming and timing the interval between the first and last received output tokens.

That revealed the real bottleneck: **processing a very long prompt before generation begins**. At around 180K context tokens, the quantized modes took roughly **two minutes to produce the first token**. Once generation started, however, they still ran at around 44 tokens/s. This distinction matters when judging how responsive the model feels in everyday use.

## Did quantization affect quality?

We did not observe a clear quality difference in these tests. All five configurations answered our 10 reasoning questions correctly and passed the *needle-in-a-haystack* retrieval checks at the tested context lengths. We then used vLLM's GSM8K evaluation (`gsm8k_eval.py --num-shots 5 --max-tokens 256`, same command for all five variants) and obtained accuracy scores between **72% and 75%**. That sample is too small to establish a statistically significant difference between the modes, but the results suggest that KV-cache quantization did **not cause a noticeable loss of accuracy** in these tests.

We also measured server throughput using the official `vllm bench serve` tool (`vllm bench serve --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2000 --random-output-len 500 --num-prompts 60 --max-concurrency 4`, same command for all five variants, just pointed at each server):

| KV-cache mode | Aggregate generation throughput |
|---|---:|
| `k3v3` | 100.4 tokens/s |
| `k3v4` | 99.9 tokens/s |
| `k3v3_compact` | 99.3 tokens/s |
| `int8_per_token_head` | 99.6 tokens/s |
| `auto` | 68.1 tokens/s |

## Which one would I use?

**For this setup, I would choose `k3v3_compact`.** It offers the largest KV-cache capacity, maintains strong generation speed with long contexts, and showed no noticeable accuracy loss in our tests. `k3v3` is a very close alternative; based on these results, it is difficult to justify using unquantized `auto`.

These findings apply to **two RX 7900 XTX GPUs and this particular vLLM build**. Other hardware or software configurations may produce a different ranking.

*Tests carried out October 10–13, 2026. Backend: [Octave, vLLM PR #59774](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59774).*

# Benchmarks — Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4 on 2x AMD RX 7900 XTX

A report with the real numbers from putting this model through its paces on the ROCm stack we have set up. It includes three methodology corrections we made along the way — the last two after review feedback — because each one changed what the numbers actually mean.

## Read this first: each KV-cache mode also changes the attention backend

This is the single most important caveat in the document, and it was missing from earlier revisions. On this stack, choosing `--kv-cache-dtype` does not only change how the KV cache is stored — **it also changes which attention backend vLLM selects**, because each backend only accepts certain cache layouts. Confirmed from the startup logs of every configuration:

| KV-cache mode | Cache storage | Attention backend selected |
|---|---|---|
| `k3v3`, `k3v4`, `k3v3_compact` | 3-bit quantized | `ROCM_OCTAVE` (the Octave backend) |
| `int8_per_token_head` | int8 | `TRITON_ATTN` |
| `auto` | fp16, unquantized | `ROCM_ATTN` |

The log line for `auto`, for example, reads:

```
Found incompatible backend(s) [TURBOQUANT, …] with AttentionType.DECODER.
Overriding with ROCM_ATTN out of potential backends: ['ROCM_ATTN', 'TRITON_ATTN']
```

(The elided entry is the Octave backend, which the stock image still reports under its older internal enum name.)

**What this means for every number below:**

- Comparisons **within** the Octave family (`k3v3` vs `k3v4` vs `k3v3_compact`) are clean: identical backend, only the packing variant differs. These are the only strictly apples-to-apples comparisons in this report.
- Comparisons **across** families (Octave vs `int8_per_token_head` vs `auto`) measure **backend and cache format together**, not quantization in isolation. A figure like "Octave is 3.8x faster than unquantized" is really "Octave-on-`ROCM_OCTAVE` is 3.8x faster than fp16-on-`ROCM_ATTN`" — a legitimate end-to-end result for this stack, but not evidence about quantization on its own.
- This is **structural, not a misconfiguration.** Octave's kernels require the quantized cache layout, so a "Octave with an unquantized cache" configuration does not exist and cannot be constructed. There is no way to isolate the quantization variable on this hardware with these backends. We checked whether `int8_per_token_head` and `auto` at least shared a backend (which would have given one matched pair) — they don't: `TRITON_ATTN` vs `ROCM_ATTN`.
- We verified this is not an eager-mode artifact: every configuration ran with `enforce_eager=False`, `cudagraph_mode=FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, and CUDA graphs captured successfully at startup (both PIECEWISE and FULL passes present in the logs).

## Methodology correction #1: decode speed vs. prefill

The first version of this report measured "long-context decode speed" with a broken formula: it estimated prefill time as `prompt_tokens / 3000` and subtracted that from the total request time to get "decode time." From ~80K tokens of context onward, that prefill estimate was far lower than real prefill (which takes tens of seconds, not a fraction), so almost all of the request time got wrongly attributed to decode — making generation speed look like it collapsed to ~1 tok/s at long context, when in reality **it stays at 40-50 tok/s for a single in-flight request**.

The fix: use streaming (`stream: true`) and measure the time between the first and last token received to get real decode speed, isolated from prefill. Time to first token (TTFT) does include the full prefill and is reported separately.

## Methodology correction #2: GSM8K was underreporting

The GSM8K numbers in the first version (72-75% accuracy) were measured through the plain `/v1/completions` endpoint with `--max-tokens 256`. For a chat-tuned model that truncates a meaningful fraction of answers before they reach the final number, depressing the measured accuracy without reflecting any real quality difference.

The fix: run the same evaluation through `/v1/chat/completions` (`--use-chat-completions`), with thinking disabled (`--chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking": false}'`) and `--max-tokens 2048`. Corrected scores land in the **97-98%** range for every variant. The relative ranking is unchanged; only the absolute numbers were wrong.

## Methodology correction #3: the long-context concurrent numbers were misread

Our first write-up of the 4-concurrent × 150K test claimed decode speed "converges to ~0.7-0.9 tok/s across all five variants," and concluded the packing variant stops mattering at long context. **That reading was wrong, and the conclusion was backwards.**

- `Output token throughput` (0.77-0.81 tok/s) divides 512 generated tokens by the full ~650s benchmark duration — and **~415s of that is prefill** (the mean TTFT). It is not a decode-rate measurement at all.
- `Mean TPOT` (~1.2s) isn't pure decode either: while one request generates, the other three are still chunked-prefilling 150K tokens each, so every decode step queues behind those prefill chunks. It measures scheduling contention, not generation speed.
- **Real decode throughput shows up in the peak**, once prefill has drained: see the corrected table below.

The corrected conclusion is the opposite of what we first wrote: at long context the choice of KV-cache mode matters **more**, not less.

## The setup

- **Model**: [`cyankiwi/Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4`](https://huggingface.co/cyankiwi/Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4) — AWQ INT4 quantization of Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid `qwen3_5` architecture: 16 full-attention layers + 48 "linear attention" / GDN layers).
- **Hardware**: 2x AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (RDNA3, gfx1100), tensor-parallel 2.
- **Build**: vLLM from the `rdna3_full_stack` branch.
- **Common flags**: `--tensor-parallel-size 2 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --max-model-len 200000 --max-num-seqs 6 --dtype float16 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml`, varying only `--kv-cache-dtype`.
- **Tests**: an informal reasoning evaluation (`temperature=0`), needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) and speed at 5 context sizes (~8K / ~30K / ~80K / ~150K / ~180K tokens) with a single in-flight request, using streaming to separate TTFT from decode speed — plus official-tool runs at short and long context under real concurrency.

## Needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH)

NIAH was run at every one of the 5 context sizes, for every variant, as part of the single-request long-context test:

| Variant | NIAH @8K | @30K | @80K | @150K | @180K |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `k3v3` | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| `k3v4` | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| `k3v3_compact` | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| `int8_per_token_head` | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| `auto` (unquantized) | pass | pass | pass | pass | *(request did not complete)* |

Every variant retrieved the needle correctly at every context length it reached. `auto` has no result at 180K because the request never finished, not because retrieval failed.

Scope caveat: NIAH tests single-fact retrieval from a long context. It does not test multi-hop reasoning that has to combine several distant parts of the context at once — the failure mode where long-context degradation usually shows up first. Our GSM8K runs use short 5-shot prompts, so they don't cover that combination either. "Long context + complex reasoning" remains untested here.

## Quality: GSM8K (corrected methodology)

`tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py` through the chat endpoint with thinking disabled and 5-shot prompting:

| Variant | GSM8K accuracy | Invalid responses |
|---|---|---|
| `k3v3_compact` | 98.0% | 0% |
| `int8_per_token_head` | 97.5% | 0% |
| `auto` (unquantized) | 97.5% | 0% |
| `k3v4` | 97.0% | 0% |
| `k3v3` | 97.0% | 0% |

The scores are close enough that this evaluation does not establish a meaningful quality difference between variants. Even `auto`, despite its very different speed profile, achieved a comparable result. These findings should not be treated as proof of identical accuracy across all tasks.

(Methodology note: the initial evaluation suffered from client-side request timeouts while requests waited behind the server's `--max-num-seqs 6` limit. We used a bounded evaluation run and increased `--request-timeout-seconds` to 900.)

## Speed at short context, real concurrency (2000 in / 500 out, 4 concurrent)

| Variant | Mean ITL | Decode per request | Aggregate throughput |
|---|---|---|---|
| `k3v3` | 33.12 ms | 30.2 tok/s | 100.4 tok/s |
| `k3v4` | 32.50 ms | 30.8 tok/s | 99.9 tok/s |
| `k3v3_compact` | 33.35 ms | 30.0 tok/s | 99.3 tok/s |
| `int8_per_token_head` | 31.67 ms | 31.6 tok/s | 99.6 tok/s |
| `auto` (unquantized) | 48.53 ms | 20.6 tok/s | 68.1 tok/s |

The three Octave variants are tied within noise (~30-31 tok/s) — a clean, same-backend comparison. `int8_per_token_head` lands in the same range on `TRITON_ATTN`. `auto` on `ROCM_ATTN` is ~32% slower.

**Caveat on the `auto` gap at this context length**: at 2000 input tokens the KV cache barely weighs anything, so cache compression alone cannot plausibly explain a 1.5x difference in per-token latency. The gap here is attributable to the backend (`ROCM_ATTN` vs the others), not to quantization. We cannot separate the two — see the opening section.

## Speed at long context, real concurrency (150,000 in / 128 out, 4 concurrent) — corrected

4 requests in flight, 150K tokens each, 600K tokens of aggregate context:

| Variant | TTFT (mean) | Peak decode throughput | Prefill-dominated avg. (not a decode rate) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `k3v3_compact` | 429.2s | **80 tok/s** | 0.79 tok/s |
| `k3v3` | 417.7s | **76 tok/s** | 0.78 tok/s |
| `k3v4` | 416.1s | **67 tok/s** | 0.81 tok/s |
| `int8_per_token_head` | 412.8s | **50 tok/s** | 0.77 tok/s |
| `auto` (unquantized) | **1226.5s** | **1 tok/s** | 0.23 tok/s |

Two things to read from this:

**1. Generation speed does not converge — it separates sharply.** Once prefill drains, the Octave variants sustain 67-80 tok/s, `int8_per_token_head` 50 tok/s, and `auto` just 1 tok/s. The ~0.7-0.9 tok/s figures in the last column are the average over the whole run including ~415s of prefill, which is why they look flat across variants; they are a measure of total job duration, not of generation speed. Our earlier revision quoted that column as if it were decode speed, and wrongly concluded the variant choice stops mattering at long context. It is the opposite: this is where the gap is widest.

**2. `auto`'s TTFT penalty at this length is partly a capacity cliff.** At 150K tokens per request, four concurrent requests need 600K tokens of KV cache — far past `auto`'s 252,671-token ceiling. The four cannot be admitted together, so they serialize, and the last waits behind three full prefill+decode cycles. That inflates its TTFT to ~3x worse (1226.5s vs ~413-429s) while the quantized variants, which hold all four, only pay the normal interleaved-prefill contention. The follow-up test in the next section removes the serialization and shows how much of the gap survives without it — most of it does.

**Relevance to our workload**: production here is 4 concurrent requests up to 32K tokens each (~128K aggregate), comfortably inside what any of these modes can admit. This 600K-aggregate scenario is a stress test well beyond it, run specifically to answer "what happens at real concurrency *and* long context" — it is not our operating point.

## Isolating the capacity cliff: 4 concurrent × 60K (240K aggregate)

The 150K test above left one variable tangled: `auto`'s 3x TTFT penalty could be its small cache forcing serialization, or a genuine throughput deficit, or both. To separate them we re-ran at **60,000 tokens per request** — 240,000 aggregate, deliberately just under `auto`'s 252,671-token ceiling, so all four requests are admitted concurrently in every mode and nothing serializes.

Both configurations reported `Peak concurrent requests: 4.00`, confirming no serialization on either side:

| Metric | `k3v3_compact` | `auto` | Ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Peak concurrent requests | 4.00 | 4.00 | — (both admitted all four) |
| Benchmark duration | 222.3s | 522.8s | 2.4x |
| Mean TTFT | 146.8s | 278.5s | 1.9x |
| **Median ITL (clean decode)** | **32.1 ms** | **531.1 ms** | **16.5x** |
| Peak decode throughput | 114 tok/s | 8 tok/s | 14x |

**The capacity cliff was not the whole story.** With serialization eliminated, `auto` is still 1.9x slower on prefill and roughly 15x slower on decode. So the 150K result's 3x TTFT gap had a capacity component, but removing it does not rescue `auto` — the underlying deficit is real and large at matched admission.

Two incidental findings worth noting:

- **Median ITL is the cleanest decode metric in these runs.** For `k3v3_compact` the mean ITL is 585 ms but the median is 32.1 ms — the mean is dragged up by the prefill contention of the other three requests, while the median reflects steps where decode actually ran unimpeded. 32.1 ms is ~31 tok/s, consistent with the short-context measurements. Where earlier revisions of this report quoted mean TPOT/ITL at long context as "decode speed", the median is the number that answers that question.
- **Prefill overhead in `auto` appears only under load.** At 8K single-request, TTFT was essentially identical between modes (6.3s vs 5.9s) — Octave adds no prefill overhead. But at 4×60K, `auto`'s prefill is 1.9x slower. Consistent with the cost of writing a much larger unquantized cache once bandwidth is contended.

As with every cross-family comparison in this report, this still bundles the attention backend with the cache format and cannot be decomposed into "how much is quantization" (see the opening section).

## The master table (single in-flight request)

| Variant | Quality | NIAH | TTFT at longest reached context | Decode ~8K / ~30K / ~80K / ~150K / ~180K | KV cache tokens ‡ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `k3v3` | pass | pass (all 5) | 121.8s at 180K | 51.4 / 51.2 / 48.8 / 45.4 / 44.4 tok/s | ~1,143,000 |
| `k3v4` | pass | pass (all 5) | 119.1s at 180K | 50.8 / 50.8 / 48.1 / 44.8 / 43.8 tok/s | ~1,006,000 |
| `k3v3_compact` | pass | pass (all 5) | 121.7s at 180K | 53.3 / 52.1 / 49.8 / 46.3 / 44.8 tok/s | ~1,385,000 |
| `int8_per_token_head` | pass | pass (all 5) | 123.0s at 180K | 50.6 / 48.1 / 41.4 / 34.3 / 31.8 tok/s | ~505,000 |
| `auto` (unquantized) | pass | pass through 150K, *did not complete 180K* | ~286s at 150K † | 14.1 at 8K; declining steeply with context † | ~252,671 ‡ |

(All `float16`, one request at a time. Note the TTFT column is not uniform: `auto`'s figure is at 150K, the others at 180K — `auto` never completed 180K. An earlier revision labelled this column "TTFT at ~180K" for all rows, which overstated the comparison.)

**† Provenance note on the `auto` row.** The raw per-length output of this run was not preserved, so unlike the four rows above it cannot be re-audited. We are reporting only what independent measurements corroborate:

- **8K: 14.1 tok/s is solid.** Independently re-measured with the same streaming method (TTFT 6.3s, decode 14.1 tok/s) — see the matched 8K comparison elsewhere in this report.
- **The steep decline with context is corroborated, but by different tests**, not by the original single-request run: at 4×60K concurrent, `auto`'s median ITL was 531 ms (~1.9 tok/s) against `k3v3_compact`'s 32.1 ms; at 4×150K concurrent, its peak decode was 1 tok/s against 67-80 tok/s. Both point the same way and at the same order of magnitude.
- **The original run's intermediate values (30K / 80K / 150K) are therefore omitted here** rather than quoted as hard figures. The qualitative claim — `auto`'s decode degrades sharply with context while the quantized modes hold roughly flat — rests on the two concurrent tests above, which are fully logged.

**‡ Capacity figures are not directly comparable across rows.** The token counts above come from separate server starts, and vLLM sizes the KV cache from whatever VRAM is free after weights and activations — which varies between runs. We confirmed this directly: two starts of the *same* `k3v3_compact` configuration reported 1,385,454 tokens (9.13 GiB available) and 1,450,909 tokens (9.55 GiB available), a 4.7% spread from run conditions alone.

The run-independent property is **bytes per token**, and it is stable: those same two `k3v3_compact` starts work out to 7,077 and 7,067 B/token — 0.14% apart. So for the one pair where we have two readings at *identical* available memory (9.13 GiB), the matched comparison is:

| Variant | Capacity at 9.13 GiB available | Bytes/token |
|---|---:|---:|
| `k3v3_compact` | 1,385,454 | ~7,070 |
| `k3v4` | 1,117,647 | ~8,770 |

That is a **1.24x** capacity advantage for `k3v3_compact` over `k3v4` at equal memory — not the 1.38x the unmatched numbers in the table imply. The ranking is robust; the magnitudes in the table's last column are inflated by run-to-run variance and should be read as approximate. We have not re-measured all five under controlled conditions, so the `k3v3`, `int8_per_token_head` and `auto` capacities are reported as-measured without a matched baseline.

## What the numbers say

### 1. Within the Octave family, `k3v3_compact` is the best choice

This is the one fully controlled comparison in the report — same backend, same everything, only the packing variant differs:

- `k3v3` and `k3v4` are equal on speed (44.4 vs 43.8 tok/s at 180K single-request; 76 vs 67 tok/s peak under long-context concurrency). `k3v4` spends more bytes per token on the value cache, so it fits less context for no speed gain.
- `k3v3_compact` is as fast or faster than `k3v3` and holds the most context of any mode — measured at ~7,070 B/token, against ~8,770 for `k3v4` (a 1.24x advantage at equal memory; see the capacity note above for why the raw token counts overstate this). It achieves that with an extra Hadamard rotation over the keys, which costs a little compute per token — but the cost does not show up as a measurable speed penalty in any of our tests.
- No meaningful quality difference was observed among the three in these evaluations.

### 2. `auto` is clearly the worst option on this stack — but attribute it correctly

`auto` is worse on every speed and capacity axis: 20.6 vs ~30 tok/s at short context, 1 vs 67-80 tok/s peak decode at 150K under concurrency, 286s TTFT at 150K single-request, 1226.5s TTFT under concurrency, and a ~252,671-token cache ceiling (roughly a quarter of the Octave variants', and the one capacity figure we re-verified directly). Critically, the matched 4×60K test shows this is **not** merely an artifact of its small cache forcing serialization: with all four requests admitted in both modes, `auto` is still 1.9x slower on prefill and ~15x slower on decode. For a long-context workload on this hardware, don't use it.

But the *reason* is a package deal: unquantized fp16 cache forces the `ROCM_ATTN` backend, and the measured gap reflects both together. We cannot report a clean "quantization gives Nx" figure from this data, and we aren't claiming one.

### 3. `int8_per_token_head` brings nothing here

It matches the Octave variants at short context (31.6 tok/s on `TRITON_ATTN`), but degrades more with context single-request (50.6 → 31.8 tok/s, -37%, vs ~-14% for Octave), peaks lower under long-context concurrency (50 vs 67-80 tok/s), and holds roughly half the cache of the Octave variants. No axis on which it wins.

### 4. TTFT is the real long-context cost, and concurrency multiplies it

Single-request TTFT grows roughly linearly with context for the quantized modes: ~6.4s at 8K, ~22s at 30K, ~60s at 80K, ~120s at 180K. Under 4-concurrent load at 150K each it rises to ~413-429s from interleaved prefill contention, and for `auto` to 1226.5s because its capacity ceiling adds forced serialization on top. In day-to-day use this — not decode speed — is what reads as "slow" in a long conversation.

## Conclusion

1. **Use a quantized KV-cache mode for long contexts.** On this stack `auto` is worse on speed and capacity at every context length we measured. Its small cache adds a serialization cliff under concurrency, but that is not the root cause: in a matched test where all four concurrent requests fit in both modes, `auto` is still 1.9x slower on prefill and ~15x slower on decode.
2. **Among the Octave variants, `k3v3_compact` is the best**: same speed as `k3v3`, more capacity than anything else. This is our recommendation, and it rests on the report's one fully controlled comparison. `k3v3` is a close, slightly simpler alternative, and the extra capacity of `k3v3_compact` is not needed at our production load — so either is defensible.
3. **`k3v4` and `int8_per_token_head` offer no advantage** over `k3v3_compact`.
4. **No meaningful quality difference was observed across the five modes** (97-98% GSM8K, NIAH pass at every reached length). These tests do not establish absolute equivalence or cover complex reasoning over long contexts.
5. **Cross-family speed comparisons in this report bundle the attention backend with the cache format**, and cannot be decomposed on this hardware. Only the within-Octave comparisons isolate the packing variant.
6. **At long context under real concurrency, the gap between modes is at its widest** (67-80 vs 50 vs 1 tok/s peak decode) — the opposite of what our previous revision concluded from a prefill-contaminated average.

RFC: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/59773

## Purpose

This adds `ROCM_OCTAVE`, an attention backend that keeps the KV cache of
full-attention layers at 3-4 bits per value, with all kernels in HIP. You
select it with `--kv-cache-dtype octave_k3v3`, `octave_k3v4` or
`octave_k3v3_compact` (216, 248 and 196 bytes per slot at head size 256,
against 1024 for fp16). The RFC explains why we built it and what we would
like it to become; `docs/design/rocm_octave.md` describes the format and the
per-architecture contract.

The short version: on 4× RX 7900 XTX with Qwen3.8-27B it holds 4.6× more
tokens than fp16 and GSM8K does not move. Against TurboQuant at the same size
it holds as many tokens or more, loses 2.5× less NLL, and runs decode 4.6×
and MTP verification 11× faster per layer at 380k, because the kernels are
written for the hardware (codebook through `v_perm_b32`, WMMA straight from
the packed cache, no host syncs). It works with MTP and CUDA graphs, and we
have served it in production since October 2, 2026.

The aim is to give ROCm a native compressed KV cache across the whole AMD
line. The capacity gain is a ratio of bytes, so it carries over to any card,
from a 24 GB Radeon to a 192 GB MI300X; the speed we have only measured on
RDNA3. There, attention stops being what grows with the context: from 128k
to 512k decode only goes from 153 to 127 tok/s, because most of the step is
the rest of the model again. This PR brings that first architecture, and the
RFC lists what the others need.

## What changes

Most of the PR is new files:

- `vllm/v1/attention/ops/rocm_octave.py`: the format and its PyTorch
  reference, which defines the byte layout.
- `vllm/v1/attention/backends/rocm_octave_attn.py`: the backend and its
  metadata builder.
- `csrc/attention/octave_*`: the kernels. Store, reduce, rotation and a
  portable decode build for every AMD target; the WMMA decode and prefill are
  for RDNA3 (gfx1100-1103).
- `tests/kernels/attention/test_rocm_octave.py`, and `--model` plus the new
  cache dtypes in `benchmarks/attention_benchmarks`.
- `docs/design/rocm_octave.md`.

The changes to existing files are small: the three cache dtypes in
`vllm/config/cache.py`, `vllm/utils/torch_utils.py` and
`vllm/v1/kv_cache_interface.py`; the backend in the registry and in the ROCm
platform's selection; the ops in `csrc/ops.h`, `csrc/torch_bindings.cpp` and
`CMakeLists.txt`. `customize_spec` now runs under the current vLLM config,
because the backend needs the model's rotary dims to size the slot. Nothing
changes for other backends or cache dtypes.

A few design choices a reviewer may want to know about:

- There is no Triton fallback. On an architecture without a native prefill
  kernel the backend refuses to start and names the missing kernel. Today
  that is everything except RDNA3; the RFC lists what each one needs.
- The metadata builder is the backend's own. It builds the per-query maps on
  the device without host syncs, supports `UNIFORM_BATCH` CUDA graphs, and
  refreshes the maps between fused MTP draft steps, so the fused draft path
  stays on.
- Supported models today: head size 256 with 64 RoPE dims, i.e. Qwen3-Next
  and Qwen3.5 / 3.6 / 3.8. The decode handles up to 8 query heads per KV head
  on each GPU, so Qwen3.5-122B and 397B need TP 4 or more. Head size 128 is
  the next step.

## Not a duplicate

I searched open PRs and issues for `splitq`, `octave`, `turboquant rocm`,
`kv cache 3-bit`, `kv cache quantization hip` and `lloyd-max kv`. The closest
are UltraQuant (#57057: FP4 with FlyDSL for gfx950, built on TurboQuant),
KVarN (#46613 / #46812: Triton, CUDA-first), #43835 (HIP int8/int4 for CDNA),
#40396 (a Triton TurboQuant decode for MI300X), #53231 (TurboQuant for Gemma 4
on ROCm) and #59132 (Triton attention for RDNA without KV quantization). None
targets RDNA with native kernels, and none runs below 8 bits with MTP on ROCm.

## Test plan

```bash
pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_rocm_octave.py -v
pre-commit run --files <changed files>
pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --files <changed python files>
```

The kernel tests compare store, decode and prefill with the PyTorch
reference for all three cache dtypes: WMMA and portable decode, 1 and 4
query tokens per request (MTP verification), padded queries, 1 to 64 KV
splits, fp16 and bf16, and prefill over a cached prefix with several
requests. To check that the tests can actually fail, I broke the kernels on
purpose a few times (a wrong codebook, a least-squares scale, a wrong `log2(e)`
in the prefill softmax, a missing query debias): each time the relevant tests
failed.

## Test results

On this branch, rebased on `main` (98b29aa99a), built for gfx1100:

- `test_rocm_octave.py`: 81 passed.
- pre-commit passes, except `update-dockerfile-graph`, which needs `/bin/bash`
  and could not run on my machine. mypy (CI stage) passes.
- End to end on this branch: Qwen3.8-27B, TP4, MTP k=3,
  `--kv-cache-dtype octave_k3v3`, nothing else from our fork. vLLM picks
  `ROCM_OCTAVE` from the cache dtype; 1,998,462 KV tokens; a needle at 45k is
  found at all three depths; GSM8K (500 questions, thinking off) 90.2 with
  0.2% invalid, MTP acceptance 85.8%, no errors in the log. The GSM8K numbers
  in the evaluation below came from our fork (91.2-92.4); the difference is
  within the noise of 500 questions (about ±1.3 points).
- One note about that run: the stock RCCL in `rocm/vllm-dev:base` cannot set
  up P2P between our 7900 XTX (`hipIpcGetMemHandle failed: invalid argument`,
  reproduced with a plain PyTorch all-reduce, without vLLM), so the image
  used a rebuilt RCCL. This is unrelated to this PR.

## Evaluation

4× RX 7900 XTX (gfx1100), Qwen3.8-27B GPTQ W4A16, TP4, 8 GB of KV cache per
GPU, same image and flags for every row. GSM8K: `tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py`,
chat, thinking off, 500 questions, temperature 0.6, no MTP so that TurboQuant
is correct. NLL: one 380k-token document.

| KV cache | Bytes | GSM8K | NLL over fp16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| fp16 | 1024 | 91.8 | — |
| `turboquant_k3v4_nc` | 230 | 89.8 | +0.00155 |
| `octave_k3v4` | 248 | 91.4 | +0.00086 |
| `octave_k3v3` | 216 | 92.4 | +0.00125 |
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | 196 | 91.8 | +0.00150 |

Attention per layer at 380k (`benchmarks/attention_benchmarks`, one TP4
shard):

| | fp16 | `turboquant_k3v4_nc` | `octave_k3v3_compact` | `octave_k3v3` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| decode, 1 token | 2370 µs | 2565 µs | 563 µs | 614 µs |
| MTP verify, 4 tokens | 48.8 ms | 6.65 ms | 0.58 ms | 0.62 ms |
| prefill, 2048-token chunk | 125.6 ms | 86.6 ms | 60.8 ms | 63.9 ms |

Time to first token, end to end with MTP and a cold prefix: 297 s at 380k
with `octave_k3v3_compact`, against 371 s with fp16 and 621 s with
TurboQuant. At 100k all three are within 8%, because the model's GEMMs and
all-reduce dominate.

When I replaced the Triton metadata builder the backend inherited at first
with its own, I checked that nothing moved (TP4, MTP, GSM8K 500 at
concurrency 6, which mixes prefill, decode and verification): GSM8K
92.2 → 91.8, MTP acceptance 83.33% → 83.39%, output 216.1 → 216.8 tok/s.

A side note on the GSM8K script: with `--max-concurrency`, its per-request
timeout also counts the time a request waits for a free connection, so queued
questions can time out and count as invalid. Our runs put a semaphore around
the request; I can send that fix separately.

## Update: sparse attention (qwen4_exp QSA)

The new commits make Octave the main KV cache of `qwen4_exp`'s sparse
attention (QSA), where each token attends to the 2048 positions its indexer
picks:

- `octave_decode_sparse`: the WMMA decode reads K/V through per-token
  top-k indices (logical positions, `-1` holes skipped) instead of a
  contiguous range. Same split-KV partials and reduce as the dense path.
- `--kv-cache-dtype octave_k3v3` / `octave_k3v4` on a QSA model sizes the
  main KV pages through `RocmOctaveAttentionBackend.customize_spec`; the QSA
  indexer pages are unchanged.
- An exact sink and recent window, a first, scoped answer to question 4 of
  the RFC (#59773). The first 4 and the last 64 tokens are also kept in fp16,
  in small direct-mapped tables keyed by cache slot and tagged, so an evicted
  entry falls back to the quantized copy. The sparse decode masks window hits
  and an exact kernel adds them as one more split before the reduce. Cost:
  ~18 MB per layer, no change in KV capacity. It lives in the QSA path only;
  the dense backend is unchanged.

Why this model needed the window: its attention is much sharper than
Qwen3.8-27B's. Q·K logits have a spread of 6-9 nats between median and p99,
the last 64 tokens take 35-80% of the attention mass in most layers, and the
first 4 take 15-40% in a few. When a few tokens carry most of the mass,
their quantization error is not averaged out over many others. Both halves
contribute: quantizing only V costs more than quantizing only K.

Evaluation: 4x RX 7900 XTX, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next GPTQ W4A16 (asymmetric, g32),
TP4, fp16, `--max-num-batched-tokens 512`, no prefix caching, same image and
flags for every row. NLL from `prompt_logprobs` over 12 code/text documents of
~8k tokens (105,910 tokens), split at position 2048 (where top-k starts to
drop tokens), and over 24 short documents (16,427 tokens). Differences are in
nats over fp16.

| KV cache | KV tokens | NLL pos >= 2048 | NLL pos < 2048 | NLL short |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fp16 | 47,409 | 1.0856 | 1.6707 | 1.1788 |
| `octave_k3v3`, no window | 155,930 | +0.0395 | +0.0851 | +0.0708 |
| `octave_k3v3` | 155,930 | +0.0163 | -0.0221 | +0.0085 |

fp16 per-token logprobs on this model vary by ~0.1 between runs (MoE and
split-K atomics); mean NLL repeats to about +-0.2% (+-0.003 nats at
pos >= 2048), so the window's pos < 2048 value is noise. These are short documents with
a different protocol from the 380k NLL above, so the two are not directly
comparable, but this model clearly costs more: the remaining +0.016 nats at
pos >= 2048 is what we are working on next. A generation eval (GSM8K) will
follow.

Note on that run: it used our fork, because the fp16 port of QSA and the RDNA3
W4A16 MoE fixes for compressed-tensors checkpoints are separate PRs (to
follow). On this branch alone the QSA path is bf16, like upstream.

Tests for this update, on this branch merged with `main` (df417f780a), built
for gfx1100:

- `test_rocm_octave.py`: 105 passed, including the new
  `test_sparse_decode_matches_reference` (window off, on, and with evicted
  entries, for the three cache dtypes and 1-2 KV heads). With the window
  removed from the reference, the 12 window cases fail and the 6 without it
  pass, so the test can tell the two apart.
- pre-commit passes on the changed files, except `update-dockerfile-graph`
  (needs `/bin/bash`, as before).

+// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
+// SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright contributors to the vLLM project
+//
+// Per-architecture primitives of the Octave kernels. Every AMD target vLLM
+// builds compiles the portable tier; faster tiers are selected at runtime by
+// the host code (see docs/design/rocm_octave.md, "Architecture contract").
+//
+//   int8 dot4: v_dot4_i32_iu8 on gfx11/gfx12, v_dot4_i32_i8 on gfx9/gfx10.3
+//   decode, fast tier: octave_decode_wmma_rdna3.cu (WMMA, gfx11)
+//   prefill: octave_prefill_rdna3.cu (WMMA, gfx11)
+//   decode, portable: octave_attn.cu decode_kernel (dot4, every target)
+//
+// The portable kernels are written for 32-lane logical waves: shuffles never
+// cross 32 lanes, so they are correct on wave64 (CDNA) as well.
+
+#pragma once
+
+#include <cstdint>
+
+namespace octave {
+
+// sum_i a.i8[i] * b.i8[i] + c, signed bytes on both sides.
+__device__ __forceinline__ int dot4_i8(int a, int b, int c) {
+#if defined(__GFX11__) || defined(__GFX12__)
+  return __builtin_amdgcn_sudot4(true, a, true, b, c, false);
+#elif defined(__gfx90a__) || defined(__gfx942__) || defined(__gfx950__) ||  \
+    defined(__gfx1030__) || defined(__gfx1031__) || defined(__gfx1032__) || \
+    defined(__gfx1033__) || defined(__gfx1034__) || defined(__gfx1035__) || \
+    defined(__gfx1036__)
+  return __builtin_amdgcn_sdot4(a, b, c, false);
+#else
+  #pragma unroll
+  for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i)
+    c += (int)(int8_t)(a >> (8 * i)) * (int)(int8_t)(b >> (8 * i));
+  return c;
+#endif
+}
+
+}  // namespace octave

+# Octave KV: a 3-bit KV cache for ROCm
+
+`ROCM_OCTAVE` is an attention backend for AMD GPUs that keeps the KV cache of
+full-attention layers at 3-4 bits per value, with native kernels (HIP today). It is
+selected with `--kv-cache-dtype octave_k3v3_compact`, `octave_k3v3` or
+`octave_k3v4` (the backend is picked from the cache dtype;
+`--attention-backend ROCM_OCTAVE` also works). The name comes from the 3-bit
+codes: each one indexes an eight-level codebook.
+
+## Why it exists
+
+Long-context serving on AMD GPUs is bounded by KV-cache memory long before it
+is bounded by compute. The existing options on ROCm were:
+
+- fp16/bf16 KV (`TRITON_ATTN`, `ROCM_ATTN`): 16 bits per value.
+- fp8 / int8 per-token-head: 8 bits per value.
+- `TURBOQUANT`: 3-4 bits per value, but its kernels are Triton (store and
+  decode) and its prefill goes through FlashAttention; it does not support the
+  fused multi-step MTP draft.
+
+Octave KV targets the same bit budget as TurboQuant with HIP kernels written for
+the AMD matrix instructions (WMMA on RDNA3, MFMA on CDNA as a contract slot),
+reading the packed cache directly in both decode and prefill, and with
+multi-token verification (MTP / speculative decoding) as a first-class case.
+
+## Supported models
+
+The format exploits *partial rotary embeddings*: models whose attention heads
+apply RoPE to a fraction of the head dims. Today the kernels are built for
+head size 256 with 64 rotary dims (`partial_rotary_factor = 0.25`), the
+attention shape of the Qwen3-Next / Qwen3.5 / Qwen3.6 / Qwen3.8 family (dense
+and MoE, e.g. Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B). Like the MLA
+backends, which serve only models with multi-head latent attention, Octave KV is
+tied to an attention shape, not to a model.
+
+Models with full RoPE (Llama, Qwen3, Mistral, ...) or other head sizes are
+rejected at startup with an explicit error. Sliding window, ALiBi, attention
+sinks, soft-capping and encoder attention are not supported.
+
+The decode kernels cover GQA groups of 1, 2, 4, 6 or 8 query heads per KV
+head on each GPU. Under tensor parallelism the group is counted per GPU, so
+models with 32 query heads and 2 KV heads (Qwen3.5-122B-A10B) need TP ≥ 4.
+
+## Format
+
+One slot per (token, KV head). V is always rotated as one 256-dim block
+(random signs, then a Walsh-Hadamard transform) and gets 3 or 4 bits per dim.
+K has two layouts:
+
+- **Block K** (`octave_k3v3`, `octave_k3v4`): four 64-dim blocks, each rotated
+  on its own. The first block holds exactly the 64 rotary dims and gets 4 bits
+  per dim, the three NoPE blocks 3 bits; each block has its own scale.
+- **Compact K** (`octave_k3v3_compact`): rotated over all 256 dims like V,
+  3 bits per dim, one scale. The rotation spreads the rotary dims over the
+  whole head, so they need no extra bits; slots pad to 4 bytes instead of 8.
+
+| Bytes (block K) | Content |
+| --- | --- |
+| `[0, 32)` | K RoPE block, 4-bit codes |
+| `[32, 104)` | K NoPE blocks, 3-bit codes |
+| next `256·v/8` | V, `v`-bit codes |
+| next 10 | fp16 scales (K blocks 0-3, V) |
+
+| Bytes (compact K) | Content |
+| --- | --- |
+| `[0, 96)` | K, 3-bit codes |
+| `[96, 192)` | V, 3-bit codes |
+| `[192, 196)` | fp16 scales (K, V) |
+
+| Cache dtype | Slot bytes | Bits per value |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `octave_k3v3_compact` | 196 | 3.06 |
+| `octave_k3v3` | 216 | 3.38 |
+| `octave_k3v4` | 248 | 3.88 |
+
+For reference, `turboquant_3bit_nc` uses 198 bytes and `turboquant_k3v4_nc`
+230.
+
+After the rotation the coordinates are close to Gaussian, so each code
+indexes the Lloyd-Max codebook of N(0, 1) for its width, stored as int8
+(`LUT` in the reference): a code `c` of a block with scale `s` stands for
+`LUT[c] · s / 64`. The scale is chosen so that `x · x̂ = |x|²`. A
+least-squares fit minimizes the reconstruction error but shrinks every
+reconstructed vector (by about 3% at 3 bits), which flattens the softmax and
+scales down the attention output; at 380k tokens it cost 2-3× more NLL than
+this scale, at the same size. The quantizer is dynamic: no calibration, no per-model
+dictionaries. The kernels map four codes to their int8 values with one
+`v_perm_b32` (two for 4-bit codes), so the codebook costs nothing in
+bandwidth and the dot products stay integer. The byte layout's source of
+truth is the PyTorch reference in `vllm/v1/attention/ops/rocm_octave.py`.
+
+Why these layouts: measured on real Q/K/V of Qwen3.8-27B (32k tokens, every
+full-attention layer, attention-output error), both K layouts sit on the same
+bytes-versus-error curve, about 25-30% below TurboQuant at equal size; block
+K reaches the 4-bit rotary block, compact K the smallest slot. Rotating the
+rotary block alone at 3 bits does not work (one layer reaches 32% error);
+rotating it with the rest of the head does. Moving bits between K and V or
+weighting K channels by query energy did not help at a fixed size. The int8
+codebook loses nothing against the floating-point one.
+
+Attention runs in the rotated space: the query is rotated like K and the
+output is rotated back once per query. The rotations are orthogonal, so the
+scores are those of the unrotated vectors.
+
+## Kernels and data flow
+
+| Step | Kernel | File |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Cache write | `octave_cache_store`: one wave per slot, rotate + quantize + pack | `csrc/attention/octave_attn.cu` |
+| Decode / MTP verify (≤128 query tokens per request) | `octave_decode`: split-KV; WMMA tier on gfx11, portable dot4 tier elsewhere; consecutive query tokens of a request share each K/V read | `octave_decode_wmma_rdna3.cu`, `octave_attn.cu` |
+| Split reduce + inverse V rotation | `reduce_kernel` | `octave_attn.cu` |
+| Prefill | `octave_prefill`: phase 1 reads the cached prefix from the packed cache (int8 WMMA for QK with per-segment scales, fp16 WMMA for PV), phase 2 attends to the chunk's own unquantized K/V and merges | `octave_prefill_rdna3.cu` |
+| Q/K/V chunk rotation for prefill | `octave_rotate` | `octave_attn.cu` |
+| Codebooks (`v_perm_b32` tables) and byte layout | — | `octave_format.cuh` |
+
+The metadata builder builds, on the device and without host syncs, the
+per-query request and causal-length maps the kernels index by. They are what
+makes MTP verification batches (several query tokens per request, each with
+its own causal length) work without special cases, and they give cudagraph
+padding queries a K length of 0.
+
+## Architecture contract
+
+Kernels are native: HIP or FlyDSL, never Triton. There is no fallback: an
+architecture without a required kernel is rejected at startup with an error
+naming what is missing. The kernels in this tree are HIP; a FlyDSL kernel
+(for example a CDNA prefill) must keep the same signature and semantics, pass
+the same tests, and report a clear error when `flydsl` is not installed.
+
+Every AMD target vLLM builds (gfx906, gfx908, gfx90a, gfx942, gfx950, gfx1030,
+gfx11xx, gfx12xx, gfx1250) compiles every Octave source; architecture-specific
+code is guarded and the portable tier uses only 32-lane shuffles, so it is
+correct on wave64 (CDNA) as well as wave32 (RDNA).
+
+| Piece | gfx1100-1103 (RDNA3) | gfx1150/1151 (RDNA3.5), gfx12 (RDNA4) | gfx90a / gfx942 / gfx950 (MI200/MI300/MI350) | gfx1030 (RDNA2) |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| int8 dot4 (`octave_arch.cuh`) | `v_dot4_i32_iu8` | `v_dot4_i32_iu8` | `v_dot4_i32_i8` | `v_dot4_i32_i8` |
+| Codebook lookup (`octave_format.cuh`) | `v_perm_b32` | `v_perm_b32` | `v_perm_b32` | `v_perm_b32` |
+| Cache store, reduce, rotate | portable | portable | portable | portable |
+| Decode | WMMA tier | portable dot4 tier | portable dot4 tier | portable dot4 tier |
+| Prefill | WMMA | **missing** | **missing** | **missing** |
+
+The WMMA kernels are compiled for gfx1100-1103 only; elsewhere they are
+empty stubs, so `_ARCH_TIERS` selects them only there. gfx1150/1151 have the
+same WMMA instructions and likely need only wider guards, but are untested.
+
+To add an architecture:
+
+1. Implement `octave_prefill` for it, in HIP or FlyDSL (same signature and semantics as
+   `octave_prefill_rdna3.cu`: phase-1 partials over the packed prefix, phase-2
+   chunk attention and merge, rotated space in and out). On CDNA the natural
+   building blocks are `v_mfma_i32_16x16x32_i8` (gfx942/gfx950) or
+   `v_mfma_f32_16x16x16f16` (gfx90a) in place of the WMMA calls.
+2. Optionally add a decode tier (the portable dot4 kernel already works).
+3. Register the tiers in `_ARCH_TIERS` in
+   `vllm/v1/attention/backends/rocm_octave_attn.py`.
+4. Run `tests/kernels/attention/test_rocm_octave.py`: every kernel is checked
+   against the PyTorch reference, and `test_decode_matches_reference` runs
+   both the fast and the portable decode tier.

+    return sq.OctaveFormat.from_cache_dtype(cache_dtype, HEAD, ROPE)

+    return ((a.float() - b.float()).norm() / b.float().norm()).item()

+def _token_slots(cache: torch.Tensor, slots: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
+    """(blocks, H, block_size, slot) cache -> (T, H, slot) for flat slots."""
+    flat = cache.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(-1, cache.shape[1], cache.shape[3])
+    return flat[slots]
+

+def _fill(cache, block_ids, k, v, k_signs, v_signs, fmt):
+    n = k.shape[0]
+    slots = (
+        block_ids.long().repeat_interleave(BLOCK)[:n] * BLOCK
+        + torch.arange(n, device=k.device) % BLOCK
+    )
+    torch.ops._C.octave_cache_store(
+        k, v, cache, slots, k_signs, v_signs, fmt.kernel_code
+    )
+    return slots

+@pytest.mark.parametrize("cache_dtype", CACHE_DTYPES)
+def test_store_matches_reference(cache_dtype):
+    torch.manual_seed(0)
+    dev, fmt = "cuda", _format(cache_dtype)
+    ksg = vsg = sq.sign_bits(HEAD).to(dev)
+    t, hkv = 1024, 2
+    k = torch.randn(t, hkv, HEAD, device=dev)
+    k[..., 100] *= 8  # an outlier channel is spread by the rotation
+    k = k.bfloat16()
+    v = torch.randn(t, hkv, HEAD, device=dev).bfloat16()
+    nblk = t // BLOCK + 4
+    cache = torch.zeros(nblk, hkv, BLOCK, fmt.slot_bytes, dtype=torch.uint8, device=dev)
+    slots = _fill(cache, torch.randperm(nblk, device=dev), k, v, ksg, vsg, fmt)
+
+    k_got, v_got = sq.reference_dequantize(_token_slots(cache, slots), fmt)
+    ref = sq.reference_quantize(k.float(), v.float(), fmt)
+    k_ref, v_ref = sq.reference_dequantize(ref, fmt)
+    # Same codes up to rounding ties from a different summation order.

+    # block) keep ~19% of the norm as error, 4-bit ~10%.
+    assert _rel(k_got, k) < 0.2

+"""Octave KV-cache format: layout, rotations and a PyTorch reference.
+
+Each (token, KV head) is stored in one byte slot. V is always quantized
+whole; K has two layouts:
+
+* Block K (``octave_k3v4``, ``octave_k3v3``): random sign flips plus a
+  Walsh-Hadamard transform over each 64-dim block. The RoPE blocks get 4-bit
+  codes, the NoPE blocks 3-bit codes, and every block has its own scale.
+* Compact K (``octave_k3v3_compact``): sign flips plus one Hadamard transform
+  over all dims, 3-bit codes, one scale. Spreading the RoPE dims over the
+  whole head lets them share the 3-bit budget.
+* V: sign flips plus one Hadamard transform over all dims, ``v_bits`` codes.
+
+The rotated coordinates are close to Gaussian, so each code indexes a
+Lloyd-Max codebook for N(0, 1), stored as int8 (``LUT``): a code ``c`` of a
+block with scale ``s`` stands for ``LUT[c] * s / LUT_ONE``. The scale makes
+``x . x_hat = |x|^2``: a least-squares fit would shrink every reconstructed
+vector, which flattens the softmax and scales down the attention output.
+Everything is computed on the fly; there is no calibration.
+
+Scores are computed in the rotated space (the query is rotated like K) and
+the attention output is rotated back once per query head.
+
+Slot layout (bytes)::
+
+    [k_rope codes][k_nope codes][v codes][fp16 scales][pad to 8]
+
+Compact K has no 4-bit part and pads to 4 bytes.
+
+4-bit codes: each little-endian uint32 covers 8 dims; byte j holds dim j in
+its low nibble and dim j + 4 in its high nibble, so ``w & 0x0F0F0F0F`` and
+``(w >> 4) & 0x0F0F0F0F`` give dims 0..3 and 4..7 as bytes.
+
+3-bit codes: a 2-bit plane (uint32 per 16 dims; ``(w >> 2i) & 0x03030303``
+gives dims 4i..4i+3) followed by a 1-bit plane (uint32 per 32 dims;
+``(w >> i) & 0x01010101`` gives dims 4i..4i+3). code = lo + 4 * hi.
+
+Scales (fp16): one per 64-dim K block (one in total for compact K), then V.

+
+
+def sign_bits(n: int) -> torch.Tensor:
+    """The sign pattern as int32 words, bit i set where the sign is -1."""
+    neg = (_signs_cpu(n) < 0).to(torch.int64).view(-1, 32)
+    words = (neg << torch.arange(32)).sum(-1)
+    return torch.where(words >= 2**31, words - 2**32, words).to(torch.int32)
+
+
+def fwht_blocks(x: torch.Tensor, block: int = HADAMARD_BLOCK) -> torch.Tensor:
+    """Orthonormal Walsh-Hadamard transform over consecutive blocks of the
+    last dim."""
+    shape = x.shape
+    y = x.reshape(-1, shape[-1] // block, block).float()
+    h = 1
+    while h < block:
+        y = y.view(*y.shape[:-1], block // (2 * h), 2, h)
+        a, b = y[..., 0, :], y[..., 1, :]
+        y = torch.stack((a + b, a - b), dim=-2).view(*y.shape[:-3], block)
+        h *= 2
+    return (y * (1.0 / math.sqrt(block))).view(shape)
+
+
+def rotate(
+    x: torch.Tensor, sgn: torch.Tensor, block: int = HADAMARD_BLOCK
+) -> torch.Tensor:
+    return fwht_blocks(x.float() * sgn, block)
+
+
+def unrotate(
+    y: torch.Tensor, sgn: torch.Tensor, block: int = HADAMARD_BLOCK
+) -> torch.Tensor:
+    return fwht_blocks(y.float(), block) * sgn
+
+
+def v_block(head_size: int) -> int:
+    """V is rotated as one block when head_size is a power of two."""
+    if head_size & (head_size - 1) == 0:
+        return head_size

+
+
+@functools.cache
+def _lut(bits: int, device_str: str) -> torch.Tensor:
+    return torch.tensor(LUT[bits], dtype=torch.float32, device=device_str)
+
+
+def _quantize_lut(x: torch.Tensor, bits: int):
+    """Nearest Lloyd-Max code on the block RMS; the scale keeps
+    ``x . x_hat = |x|^2``.
+
+    Returns (codes uint8 in [0, 2**bits), scale) with
+    x ≈ LUT[codes] * scale / LUT_ONE.
+    """
+    lut = _lut(bits, str(x.device))
+    ss = x.pow(2).sum(-1, keepdim=True)
+    rms = (ss / x.shape[-1]).sqrt().clamp_min(1e-12)
+    y = x / rms * LUT_MULT[bits]
+    codes = torch.bucketize(y, (lut[1:] + lut[:-1]) / 2)
+    dot = (x * lut[codes]).sum(-1, keepdim=True)
+    scale = torch.where(dot > 0, ss / dot.clamp_min(1e-30), 0.0) * LUT_ONE
+    return codes.to(torch.uint8), scale
+
+
+def _pack(codes: torch.Tensor, bits: int) -> torch.Tensor:
+    """codes: (..., n) uint8 -> (..., n * bits / 8) uint8, layout above."""
+    c = codes.to(torch.int64)
+    if bits == 4:
+        g = c.view(*c.shape[:-1], -1, 2, 4)  # (word, half, byte)
+        b = g[..., 0, :] | (g[..., 1, :] << 4)
+        return b.reshape(*c.shape[:-1], -1).to(torch.uint8)
+    lo = (c & 3).view(*c.shape[:-1], -1, 4, 4)  # (word, i, byte)
+    lo_b = (lo << (2 * torch.arange(4, device=c.device)).view(4, 1)).sum(-2)
+    hi = (c >> 2).view(*c.shape[:-1], -1, 8, 4)
+    hi_b = (hi << torch.arange(8, device=c.device).view(8, 1)).sum(-2)
+    return torch.cat(
+        (lo_b.reshape(*c.shape[:-1], -1), hi_b.reshape(*c.shape[:-1], -1)), -1
+    ).to(torch.uint8)
+

+def _unpack(packed: torch.Tensor, n: int, bits: int) -> torch.Tensor:
+    p = packed.to(torch.int64)
+    if bits == 4:
+        g = p.view(*p.shape[:-1], -1, 4)
+        c = torch.stack((g & 15, g >> 4), dim=-2)
+        return c.reshape(*p.shape[:-1], n)
+    lo_bytes = n // 4
+    lo = p[..., :lo_bytes].view(*p.shape[:-1], -1, 1, 4)
+    lo = (lo >> (2 * torch.arange(4, device=p.device)).view(4, 1)) & 3
+    hi = p[..., lo_bytes:].view(*p.shape[:-1], -1, 1, 4)
+    hi = (hi >> torch.arange(8, device=p.device).view(8, 1)) & 1
+    return lo.reshape(*p.shape[:-1], n) + 4 * hi.reshape(*p.shape[:-1], n)
+
+
+def reference_quantize(
+    key: torch.Tensor, value: torch.Tensor, fmt: OctaveFormat
+) -> torch.Tensor:
+    """(T, H, D) K and V -> (T, H, slot_bytes) uint8 slots."""
+    t, h, d = key.shape
+    r, dev = fmt.rope_dim, key.device
+    out = torch.zeros(t, h, fmt.slot_bytes, dtype=torch.uint8, device=dev)
+    nkb = fmt.num_k_blocks
+
+    if fmt.compact:
+        k = rotate(key, signs(d, str(dev)), d)
+        k_codes, k_scale = _quantize_lut(k, NOPE_BITS)
+        out[..., : fmt.off_v] = _pack(k_codes, NOPE_BITS)
+    else:
+        k = rotate(key, signs(d, str(dev))).view(t, h, nkb, HADAMARD_BLOCK)
+        nr = fmt.num_rope_blocks
+        kr_codes, kr_scale = _quantize_lut(k[:, :, :nr], ROPE_BITS)
+        kn_codes, kn_scale = _quantize_lut(k[:, :, nr:], NOPE_BITS)
+        out[..., : fmt.off_k_nope] = _pack(kr_codes.view(t, h, r), ROPE_BITS)
+        out[..., fmt.off_k_nope : fmt.off_v] = _pack(
+            kn_codes.view(t, h, fmt.nope_dim), NOPE_BITS
+        )
+        k_scale = torch.cat((kr_scale[..., 0], kn_scale[..., 0]), -1)
+
+    vr = rotate(value, signs(d, str(dev)), v_block(d))
+    v_codes, v_scale = _quantize_lut(vr, fmt.v_bits)
+    out[..., fmt.off_v : fmt.off_scales] = _pack(v_codes, fmt.v_bits)
+
+    scales = torch.cat((k_scale, v_scale), -1)
+    sc = scales.to(torch.float16).view(torch.uint8).view(t, h, -1)
+    out[..., fmt.off_scales : fmt.off_scales + sc.shape[-1]] = sc
+    return out
+
+
+def reference_dequantize(
+    slots: torch.Tensor, fmt: OctaveFormat, rotated: bool = False
+) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
+    """(T, H, slot) slots -> fp32 K and V of shape (T, H, D).
+
+    With ``rotated=True`` K and V stay in the rotated space, which is what
+    the kernels consume.
+    """
+    t, h, _ = slots.shape
+    r, d, dev = fmt.rope_dim, fmt.head_size, slots.device
+    sc = (
+        slots[..., fmt.off_scales : fmt.off_scales + 2 * fmt.num_scales]
+        .contiguous()
+        .view(torch.float16)
+        .float()
+        / LUT_ONE
+    )
+    if fmt.compact:
+        k = _unpack(slots[..., : fmt.off_v], d, NOPE_BITS)
+        k = _lut(NOPE_BITS, str(dev))[k] * sc[..., :1]
+    else:
+        kr = _unpack(slots[..., : fmt.off_k_nope], r, ROPE_BITS)
+        kn = _unpack(slots[..., fmt.off_k_nope : fmt.off_v], fmt.nope_dim, NOPE_BITS)
+        k = torch.cat(
+            (_lut(ROPE_BITS, str(dev))[kr], _lut(NOPE_BITS, str(dev))[kn]), -1
+        ).view(t, h, fmt.num_k_blocks, HADAMARD_BLOCK)
+        k = (k * sc[..., : fmt.num_k_blocks, None]).view(t, h, d)
+
+    v = _unpack(slots[..., fmt.off_v : fmt.off_scales], d, fmt.v_bits)
+    v = _lut(fmt.v_bits, str(dev))[v] * sc[..., -1:]
+    if not rotated:
+        k = unrotate(k, signs(d, str(dev)), fmt.k_rotation_block)
+        v = unrotate(v, signs(d, str(dev)), v_block(d))
+    return k, v
+
+
+def reference_attention(
+    query: torch.Tensor,
+    cache: torch.Tensor,
+    block_table: torch.Tensor,
+    q_to_req: torch.Tensor,
+    q_to_klen: torch.Tensor,
+    fmt: OctaveFormat,
+    scale: float,
+) -> torch.Tensor:
+    """Per-query-token attention over a Octave paged cache.
+
+    query: (Q, Hq, D). cache: (num_blocks, Hkv, block_size, slot) uint8.
+    Query token i attends to the first ``q_to_klen[i]`` tokens of request
+    ``q_to_req[i]``.
+    """
+    num_q, hq, d = query.shape
+    _, hkv, block_size, _ = cache.shape
+    group = hq // hkv
+    out = torch.zeros(num_q, hq, d, dtype=torch.float32, device=query.device)
+    for i in range(num_q):
+        klen = int(q_to_klen[i])
+        if klen <= 0:
+            continue
+        req = int(q_to_req[i])
+        pos = torch.arange(klen, device=cache.device)
+        blocks = block_table[req, pos // block_size].long()
+        slots = cache[blocks, :, pos % block_size]  # (klen, Hkv, slot)
+        k, v = reference_dequantize(slots, fmt)
+        k = k.repeat_interleave(group, dim=1)
+        v = v.repeat_interleave(group, dim=1)
+        s = torch.einsum("hd,thd->ht", query[i].float(), k) * scale
+        p = torch.softmax(s, dim=-1)
+        out[i] = torch.einsum("ht,thd->hd", p, v)
+    return out

# Qwen3.8-27B on Dual RX 7900 XTX: Benchmarking KV Cache Quantization in vLLM

I wanted to see how well Qwen3.8-27B would run on two AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX GPUs (24 GB each), especially during long conversations. The goal was straightforward: reduce GPU memory usage by quantizing the KV cache, while keeping generation speed and answer quality as close as possible to the unquantized setup.

I compared five KV-cache configurations in vLLM, all using `float16` and tensor parallelism across both GPUs. Three packing variants—`k3v3`, `k3v4`, and `k3v3_compact`—use our RDNA3 backend, **Octave** ([vLLM PR #59774](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59774)). `int8_per_token_head` uses a separate quantized kernel implementation, while `auto` leaves the KV cache unquantized. The model was [`cyankiwi/Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4`](https://huggingface.co/cyankiwi/Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4).

## Main results

| KV-cache mode | Generation speed at ~180K context tokens | KV-cache capacity (tokens) | GSM8K accuracy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **`k3v3_compact`** | **44.8 tokens/s** | **1,385,454** | **75%** |
| `k3v3` | 44.4 tokens/s | 1,143,333 | 74% |
| `k3v4` | 43.8 tokens/s | 1,005,882 | 75% |
| `int8_per_token_head` | 31.8 tokens/s | 505,185 | 72% |
| `auto` (unquantized) | Test not completed | 252,671 | 73% |

The three Octave variants sustained roughly **44–45 tokens/s even with ~180K tokens of context**. `k3v3_compact` also provided the highest KV-cache capacity. The separate INT8 implementation slowed down more at long context lengths, while unquantized `auto` performed substantially worse.

The capacity figures above describe the **aggregate KV-cache token capacity reported by vLLM**, not the maximum length of a single conversation. For these tests, `--max-model-len` was set to **200,000 tokens**.

One important correction came out of the testing. Our first measurements made long-context generation look extremely slow, but the issue was in our benchmark script rather than the quantized cache. We estimated how long prompt processing (*prefill*) would take and accidentally counted much of that time as generation. We fixed the measurement by using streaming and timing the interval between the first and last received output tokens.

That revealed the real bottleneck: **processing a very long prompt before generation begins**. At around 180K context tokens, the quantized modes took roughly **two minutes to produce the first token**. Once generation started, however, they still ran at around 44 tokens/s. This distinction matters when judging how responsive the model feels in everyday use.

## Did quantization affect quality?

We did not observe a clear quality difference in these tests. All five configurations answered our 10 reasoning questions correctly and passed the *needle-in-a-haystack* retrieval checks at the tested context lengths. We then used vLLM's GSM8K evaluation (`gsm8k_eval.py --num-shots 5 --max-tokens 256`, same command for all five variants) and obtained accuracy scores between **72% and 75%**. That sample is too small to establish a statistically significant difference between the modes, but the results suggest that KV-cache quantization did **not cause a noticeable loss of accuracy** in these tests.

We also measured server throughput using the official `vllm bench serve` tool (`vllm bench serve --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2000 --random-output-len 500 --num-prompts 60 --max-concurrency 4`, same command for all five variants, just pointed at each server):

| KV-cache mode | Aggregate generation throughput |
|---|---:|
| `k3v3` | 100.4 tokens/s |
| `k3v4` | 99.9 tokens/s |
| `k3v3_compact` | 99.3 tokens/s |
| `int8_per_token_head` | 99.6 tokens/s |
| `auto` | 68.1 tokens/s |

## Which one would I use?

**For this setup, I would choose `k3v3_compact`.** It offers the largest KV-cache capacity, maintains strong generation speed with long contexts, and showed no noticeable accuracy loss in our tests. `k3v3` is a very close alternative; based on these results, it is difficult to justify using unquantized `auto`.

These findings apply to **two RX 7900 XTX GPUs and this particular vLLM build**. Other hardware or software configurations may produce a different ranking.

*Tests carried out October 10–13, 2026. Backend: [Octave, vLLM PR #59774](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59774).*

# Benchmarks — Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4 on 2x AMD RX 7900 XTX

A report with the real numbers from putting this model through its paces on the ROCm stack we have set up. It includes three methodology corrections we made along the way — the last two after review feedback — because each one changed what the numbers actually mean.

## Read this first: each KV-cache mode also changes the attention backend

This is the single most important caveat in the document, and it was missing from earlier revisions. On this stack, choosing `--kv-cache-dtype` does not only change how the KV cache is stored — **it also changes which attention backend vLLM selects**, because each backend only accepts certain cache layouts. Confirmed from the startup logs of every configuration:

| KV-cache mode | Cache storage | Attention backend selected |
|---|---|---|
| `k3v3`, `k3v4`, `k3v3_compact` | 3-bit quantized | `ROCM_OCTAVE` (the Octave backend) |
| `int8_per_token_head` | int8 | `TRITON_ATTN` |
| `auto` | fp16, unquantized | `ROCM_ATTN` |

The log line for `auto`, for example, reads:

```
Found incompatible backend(s) [TURBOQUANT, …] with AttentionType.DECODER.

**What this means for every number below:**

- Comparisons **within** the Octave family (`k3v3` vs `k3v4` vs `k3v3_compact`) are clean: identical backend, only the packing variant differs. These are the only strictly apples-to-apples comparisons in this report.
- Comparisons **across** families (Octave vs `int8_per_token_head` vs `auto`) measure **backend and cache format together**, not quantization in isolation. A figure like "Octave is 3.8x faster than unquantized" is really "Octave-on-`ROCM_OCTAVE` is 3.8x faster than fp16-on-`ROCM_ATTN`" — a legitimate end-to-end result for this stack, but not evidence about quantization on its own.
- This is **structural, not a misconfiguration.** Octave's kernels require the quantized cache layout, so a "Octave with an unquantized cache" configuration does not exist and cannot be constructed. There is no way to isolate the quantization variable on this hardware with these backends. We checked whether `int8_per_token_head` and `auto` at least shared a backend (which would have given one matched pair) — they don't: `TRITON_ATTN` vs `ROCM_ATTN`.
- We verified this is not an eager-mode artifact: every configuration ran with `enforce_eager=False`, `cudagraph_mode=FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, and CUDA graphs captured successfully at startup (both PIECEWISE and FULL passes present in the logs).

## Methodology correction #1: decode speed vs. prefill

The first version of this report measured "long-context decode speed" with a broken formula: it estimated prefill time as `prompt_tokens / 3000` and subtracted that from the total request time to get "decode time." From ~80K tokens of context onward, that prefill estimate was far lower than real prefill (which takes tens of seconds, not a fraction), so almost all of the request time got wrongly attributed to decode — making generation speed look like it collapsed to ~1 tok/s at long context, when in reality **it stays at 40-50 tok/s for a single in-flight request**.

The fix: use streaming (`stream: true`) and measure the time between the first and last token received to get real decode speed, isolated from prefill. Time to first token (TTFT) does include the full prefill and is reported separately.

## Methodology correction #2: GSM8K was underreporting

The GSM8K numbers in the first version (72-75% accuracy) were measured through the plain `/v1/completions` endpoint with `--max-tokens 256`. For a chat-tuned model that truncates a meaningful fraction of answers before they reach the final number, depressing the measured accuracy without reflecting any real quality difference.

The fix: run the same evaluation through `/v1/chat/completions` (`--use-chat-completions`), with thinking disabled (`--chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking": false}'`) and `--max-tokens 2048`. Corrected scores land in the **97-98%** range for every variant. The relative ranking is unchanged; only the absolute numbers were wrong.

## Methodology correction #3: the long-context concurrent numbers were misread

Our first write-up of the 4-concurrent × 150K test claimed decode speed "converges to ~0.7-0.9 tok/s across all five variants," and concluded the packing variant stops mattering at long context. **That reading was wrong, and the conclusion was backwards.**

- `Output token throughput` (0.77-0.81 tok/s) divides 512 generated tokens by the full ~650s benchmark duration — and **~415s of that is prefill** (the mean TTFT). It is not a decode-rate measurement at all.
- `Mean TPOT` (~1.2s) isn't pure decode either: while one request generates, the other three are still chunked-prefilling 150K tokens each, so every decode step queues behind those prefill chunks. It measures scheduling contention, not generation speed.
- **Real decode throughput shows up in the peak**, once prefill has drained: see the corrected table below.

The corrected conclusion is the opposite of what we first wrote: at long context the choice of KV-cache mode matters **more**, not less.
